Lower bounds / separations — there is a family achieving this

  • \(\mathrm{N}_p(\mathrm{PARITY}_n) = \Theta(n\log n)\)
    witness: \(\oplus_n\) FRPU94 EvansPippenger98
    So the $\log$ is genuinely necessary: $\mathrm{N}_p$ is not $\Theta(\mathrm{R})$.
  • \(\text{almost every } f:\ \mathrm{N}_p(f) = \Omega(n\log n)\)
    ReischukSchmeltz91

High total influence is what forces the $\log$: $\mathrm{N}_p(f)=\Theta(n\log n)$ whenever $\mathrm{I}(f)=\Omega(n)$ [Gu25noisy], and since 2026 the scale-free version $\mathrm{N}_p(f)=\Omega(\mathrm{I}(f)\log \mathrm{I}(f))$ holds for every total $f$ [GLX26noisy] -- see the $\mathrm{I}\to\mathrm{N}_p$ record. The quantum analogue behaves differently: $\mathrm{Q}^{\mathrm{rob}}(\mathrm{PARITY}_n)=\Theta(n)$ with no log [BNRdW05].

see also: \(\mathrm{N}_{p}(f)\), \(\mathrm{R}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), \(\mathrm{Q}^{\mathrm{rob}}(f)\), \(\mathrm{I}(f)\), \(\oplus_n\), Two different noisy query models data/relations/04-composition.yaml

lo.note: Theorem 1, for every (possibly partial) Boolean $f$: against the hardest input distribution, unlimited correlated samples are worth nothing. The obstruction is the [Shaltiel04] examples -- distributions with a small easy part, which many samples let you hunt for -- and the proof builds hard distributions with no easy part, via likelihood boosters: a decision tree that with probability $\ge 1-\delta$ multiplies the likelihood ratio between $D_0^k$ and $D_1^k$ by at most $M$. [BenDavidBlais20minimax] reprove it from their Shaltiel-free minimax theorems.
Corollary 1, immediately from $\mathrm{Corr}(f,D) = O(\mathrm{Sel}(f,D))$ and $\mathrm{R} = O(\mathrm{Corr})$.

Upper bounds — holds for every relation

  • \(\mathrm{N}_p(f) = O\!\left(\frac{\mathrm{R}(f)\log \mathrm{R}(f)}{(1-2p)^2}\right)\)
    FRPU94
    The $p$-dependence is the usual $1/(1-2p)^2$ Chernoff factor; the interesting content is the $\log \mathrm{R}$. The proof simulates each clean query by the majority of $O(\log \mathrm{R}/(1-2p)^2)$ noisy copies and union-bounds over the $\mathrm{R}$ queries, which is a statement about the oracle, not about the output: it holds verbatim for partial functions and relations.

For any constant $p<1/2$ the measure $\mathrm{N}_p$ is the same up to constants, which is why the subscript is usually dropped. As $p\to 1/2$ it degenerates in the same way $\mathrm{R}_{1/2-\gamma}$ does. See Two different noisy query models for the contrast with $\mathrm{noisyR}$, where the algorithm chooses a bias per query and pays $\gamma^2$ for it.

see also: \(\mathrm{N}_{p}(f)\), \(\mathrm{noisyR}(f)\), \(\mathrm{R}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), \(\mathrm{Q}^{\mathrm{rob}}(f)\), Two different noisy query models data/relations/07-parameters.yaml

params.name: p
params.dependence: For constant $p$, changing $p$ changes $\mathrm{N}_p$ by only a constant factor (each "reliable" bit costs $\Theta(\log(1/\delta)/(1-2p)^2)$ repetitions). The interesting dependence is on the target error and on $n$.

facts: $\mathrm{N}_p(f) = O(\mathrm{R}(f)\log \mathrm{R}(f))$ always (amplify each query by $O(\log \mathrm{R})$ repetitions and union bound).
$\mathrm{N}_p(\mathrm{PARITY}_n) = \Theta(n\log n)$ [FRPU94] -- the log factor is necessary, giving a genuine separation from $\mathrm{R}$.

$\mathrm{N}_p(f) = \Omega(\mathrm{I}(f)\log \mathrm{I}(f))$ for every total $f$ [GLX26noisy] -- the first general lower bound beyond the trivial $\mathrm{N}_p(f) = \Omega(\mathrm{R}(f))$, and tight at PARITY.
Almost all $f$ need $\Omega(n\log n)$ noisy queries [Reischuk-Schmeltz].
Quantum contrast: the robust quantum query complexity of PARITY is $\Theta(n)$ -- no log factor [BNRdW05].

lo.note:
A single character has sparsity $1$ and $\mathrm{osss} = 1$: the two agree, but neither
grows, so this witnesses no exponent. No function in the zoo has $\mathrm{osss}$ growing
while $\mathrm{spar}$ stays bounded -- indeed $\mathrm{spar}(f) = O(1)$ forces $f$ to be a
constant-size combination of characters, and $\mathrm{osss}$ is then bounded too.

lo.chip_name: a family with M1 = Omega-tilde(M2^a): tight up to logs
lo.note: Via subcube partition complexity, $\mathrm{prt} \le \mathrm{SP}$: [AKK16] give a total $f$ with $\mathrm{D}(f) = \tilde\Omega(\mathrm{SP}(f)^2)$. This is nearly the most that can happen, since $\mathrm{D}(f) = O(\mathrm{prt}_0(f)\,\mathrm{prt}_{1/3}(f))$ [JainKlauck10, Thm 3.7].
